title: Relic
summary: Upload an old codebase as a zip file and get a written report: an overview, three diagrams, a note on every file, and answers that show which lines they came from.
role: Design and development of the analysis pipeline, the API and the interface.
description: Taking over an old codebase starts with weeks of reading. Relic shortens that: upload the code as a zip file and it returns a written overview of the system, three diagrams (architecture, data flow and dependencies) and a note on every file. After that it answers questions from the code itself, and shows under each answer which files and lines it used.

It is a working prototype: the uploaded code is held in memory for an hour, finished reports are saved, and there are no accounts yet. The overview and the notes are written by an AI model and can be wrong; the dependency diagram and the counts are not.

I reworked it in 2026. The interface used to be a chat window with the upload behind a small button; now the upload and the report are the page. Behind it, reports are no longer cut off, the progress is real, and a larger project takes a few minutes on a free AI account instead of failing. The pictures show it reading an old PHP course project of mine, 49 files.

highlights.title: A core sample of the upload
highlights.text: Before anything is analysed, the upload is drawn the way a geologist shows a drill core: one column whose layers are the languages in the zip, each as tall as its share of the bytes.

highlights.title: Answers that show their sources
highlights.text: A question is matched against the uploaded code by a keyword ranking written by hand, with no embeddings. A page that matches brings along the script its form posts to. The model is told to answer only from the lines it was given, and those lines are listed under the answer.

highlights.title: Built for a small allowance
highlights.text: A free account of the AI service allows 8,000 tokens a minute. Relic sizes every request to fit, condenses the notes folder by folder when they are too many, and spaces its requests so that none is refused. It says beforehand how long that will take: nine minutes estimated for 49 files, and nine to ten measured.

highlights.title: Structure first, model second
highlights.text: The code is parsed before any model sees it. Imports, functions and classes are sent in batches, and the files are ranked first, so entry points and files that many others import get their note before tests and generated files.

highlights.title: Diagrams that render
highlights.text: The dependency diagram comes from the import and include statements of Python, JavaScript, TypeScript and PHP files, not from the model. The two diagrams the model writes follow strict syntax rules and are cleaned before they reach the page.

highlights.title: Uploads it does not trust
highlights.text: Size limits before and after unpacking, a compression-ratio check, a cap on the number of entries and a check against paths that climb out of the folder.
